newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma blasts U.S. for "nonsense" rights report.
newsitem.headline: Burma blasts U.S. for "nonsense" rights report.

text.p: Burma hit back on Friday at the United States for its accusations of human rights abuses in Burma, saying they were "nonsense" and part of a conspiracy against the Southeast Asian nation.

In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department said severe human rights repression by Burma's military regime increased during 1996, despite strong economic activity that gave the appearance of normalcy.

"Those who issued this so-called Human Rights Practices Report ... are either extremely ignorant of the true situation in Myanmar (Burma) or they are following an aggressive policy to discredit the Myanmar government in the eyes of the international world by using unscrupulous means and ways," a government spokesman told Reuters from Rangoon.
Calling the report a "conspiracy agaist Myanmar," he said it was just one of many similar accusations made against Burma.
"The silent majority who know and understand Myanmar's situation is truly fed up with all the disinformation disseminated by the people with ill intent," he said.
"They have expressed their desire to see the sole superpower nation follow a more consistent and a non-double standard policy towards every nation of the world."
The report faulted the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) for restricting the democratic opposition -- the National League for Democracy (NLD) and its leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
The NLD won a landslide victory in a 1990 election but the SLORC never allowed it to take office.
The report cited "credible reports" of brutality and killings of civilians by the military, especially in areas dominated by ethnic minorities.
"Out of sight of most visitors, citizens continued to live subject at any time and without appeal to the arbitrary and sometimes brutal dictates of the military dictatorship," the report said.
It said arbitrary arrests and detentions continued for expression of dissenting political views.
"Several hundred, if not more, political prisoners remained in detention, including approximately 20 members of parliament elected in 1990," the report said.
Burmese exiles in Thailand welcomed the U.S. report.
"We welcome this human rights report by the U.S. government," said Zaw Min, foreign affairs spokesman for the All Burma Student Democratic Front. "We support the criticism of the SLORC."
Zaw Min said he hoped the report was the first step for the U.S. government to implement economic sanctions on Burma.

The U.S. Senate has approved a bill that gives President Bill Clinton the authority to impose economic sanctions on Burma if the political situation there deteriorates or if there are serious threats to Aung San Suu Kyi.
